title: Squeeze Out Repeats In Place
statement:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order, so equal values sit next to each other. Let k be the number of distinct values in it.

Rearrange nums in place so that its first k slots hold each distinct value once, in increasing order. Do not create a second array; overwrite the existing one. What is left in the slots after index k − 1 does not matter, and the length of the array stays the same.

In the classic version the function also returns k. Here the function returns nothing: the checker works out k itself and reads the first k slots of your array.

examples.why: Four distinct values, so k = 4. The underscores can be anything.
Negative values and zero work the same way. Each run collapses to one copy.
One distinct value: only the first slot is checked.

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Because the array is sorted, a value is new exactly when it differs from the value just before it.
Keep two indexes: one reads every element, the other marks where the next new value should be written.
Write index k starts at 1. For each i from 1, if nums[i] differs from nums[k − 1], copy it to nums[k] and move k forward.

explain.intuition:
Sorting puts all copies of a value side by side, so "is this value new?" only needs one comparison with the last value you kept. No set, no lookups.

Use a reader and a writer. The reader i visits every element. The writer k points at the next free slot in the clean prefix. When the reader sees a value different from nums[k − 1], the last value written, it copies it to nums[k] and the writer moves on. The writer never passes the reader, so nothing is overwritten before it is read.
steps: Set k = 1: the first element is always kept.
For i from 1 to n − 1: if nums[i] !== nums[k − 1], set nums[k] = nums[i] and add one to k.
The first k slots now hold the distinct values.
pitfalls: Comparing with nums[i − 1] after you have started overwriting. It still works here only because the writer is never ahead of the reader; comparing with nums[k − 1] says what you mean.
Calling splice for every duplicate. Each call shifts the rest of the array, which makes the loop O(n²).
Building a new array with new Set(nums) and assigning it to the parameter. The caller's array is unchanged.

solutions.title: Shift left on every repeat
solutions.idea: Whenever a value equals the one before it, shift everything after it one slot left. Simple, but each shift is O(n).

solutions.title: Reader and writer pointers
solutions.idea: One index reads every value; the other writes each new value into the next free slot of the clean prefix.

followups: Allow each value to appear at most twice. What single change to the comparison does it?
The array is not sorted. Can you still keep only first occurrences in place, and what does it cost?
